misconceptions.statement: If a line starts at the 1 cm mark and ends at 6 cm, its length is 6 cm.
misconceptions.why: Students read only the end number and ignore where the segment starts on the ruler.
misconceptions.fix: Length is the difference between the two readings, so 6 minus 1 is 5 cm. It is easier to place the zero mark at one end.

probe.question: A segment starts at the 2 cm mark and ends at the 9 cm mark on a ruler. What is its length?
probe.wrong_answer: 9 cm

misconceptions.root_belief: the end reading is the whole measurement
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom studies of children's errors in measuring length with a ruler

misconceptions.statement: After picking up a length with the compass, you can change its opening a little while drawing.
misconceptions.why: Students see the compass as a loose drawing tool and do not treat the opening as a stored measurement.
misconceptions.fix: The opening is the length being copied, so it must stay fixed from picking the length up until the arc is drawn.

probe.question: You set a compass to 5 cm and then loosen it slightly before drawing the arc. Does the arc still have radius 5 cm?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a small change does not matter

misconceptions.root_belief: steps in a procedure can be changed freely

misconceptions.statement: To draw a triangle from three sides, both arcs from the ends of the base must have the same radius.
misconceptions.why: Students remember the equilateral or perpendicular-bisector steps where both arcs are equal and apply them to every triangle.
misconceptions.fix: Each arc has the radius of one of the other two sides. They are equal only if those two sides are equal in length.

probe.question: To construct a triangle with sides 6 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, you draw the 6 cm base. What radii do you use for the two arcs?
probe.wrong_answer: Both arcs of 4 cm, or both of 5 cm

misconceptions.root_belief: steps that look alike use the same values

misconceptions.statement: Any compass opening works for the arcs when drawing a perpendicular bisector.
misconceptions.why: Students follow the steps by habit and do not see why the arcs must cross each other.
misconceptions.fix: The opening must be more than half the segment length, or the arcs will not meet. Using the same opening from both ends makes the crossing points equally far from both ends.

probe.question: For a 10 cm segment you draw arcs of radius 3 cm from both ends. Will they cross?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, any radius works

misconceptions.root_belief: details of a procedure do not matter
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of procedural versus conceptual understanding in geometric constructions

misconceptions.statement: A perpendicular bisector only needs to be at right angles to the segment, wherever it touches it.
misconceptions.why: Students remember 'perpendicular' and drop the 'bisector' part.
misconceptions.fix: A perpendicular bisector is at 90 degrees to the segment and also passes through its midpoint, cutting it into two equal parts.

probe.question: A line is perpendicular to PQ and meets it at a point 2 cm from P, with PQ = 8 cm. Is it the perpendicular bisector?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is perpendicular

misconceptions.root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Any line passing through the midpoint of a segment is its perpendicular bisector.
misconceptions.why: Students picture a line through the middle without checking the angle.
misconceptions.fix: Many lines pass through the midpoint, but only the one at 90 degrees to the segment is its perpendicular bisector.

probe.question: A slanting line passes through the midpoint of AB. Is it the perpendicular bisector of AB?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it goes through the midpoint

misconceptions.root_belief: passing through the middle is enough

misconceptions.statement: A point far up on the perpendicular bisector of AB is closer to one end than the other.
misconceptions.why: Students judge by the look of the diagram and think the distances change as you move away from the segment.
misconceptions.fix: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is the same distance from A as from B, however far from the segment it is.

probe.question: P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB and PA = 7 cm. What is PB?
probe.wrong_answer: Cannot say, it is different from 7 cm

misconceptions.root_belief: what looks unequal in the picture is unequal

misconceptions.statement: The angle bisector is the line joining the midpoints of the two arms.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'bisect' means 'find the middle' and take the middle of each arm.
misconceptions.fix: The bisector is a ray from the vertex that splits the angle into two equal angles. It is found by arcs, not by joining midpoints of the arms.

probe.question: An angle has arms of length 4 cm and 10 cm. You join their midpoints. Is this line the angle bisector?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is in the middle of the arms

misconceptions.root_belief: the middle of the picture is the middle of the idea

misconceptions.statement: An angle with longer arms is a bigger angle.
misconceptions.why: Students compare how much of the drawing is covered, not the amount of opening.
misconceptions.fix: Angle size is the amount of opening between the arms. Making the arms longer or shorter does not change it.

probe.question: Angle A has 3 cm arms and angle B has 8 cm arms, and both open the same amount. Which is bigger?
probe.wrong_answer: Angle B

misconceptions.root_belief: a bigger drawing means a bigger measure
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's concept of angle as arm length or area

misconceptions.statement: In the 60 degree construction, the second arc can have any radius.
misconceptions.why: Students do not know that the two arcs form an equilateral triangle, so they see no reason for equal radii.
misconceptions.fix: The second arc must use the same radius as the first, so the vertex, the arc point and the crossing point form an equilateral triangle with 60 degree angles.

probe.question: After drawing the first arc of radius 4 cm from O, you draw the second arc from the arc point with radius 6 cm. Is the angle 60 degrees?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is still 60 degrees

misconceptions.root_belief: details of a procedure do not matter

misconceptions.statement: On a protractor you can always read the angle from the inner scale.
misconceptions.why: Students read the scale nearest to them instead of the one starting at zero on the arm.
misconceptions.fix: Read the scale that starts at 0 on the arm lying along the baseline. If the arm points to the other side, use the other scale.

probe.question: The baseline arm points to the 0 on the outer scale. The other arm passes the outer 40 and inner 140. What is the angle?
probe.wrong_answer: 140 degrees

misconceptions.root_belief: always use the first or nearest option
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of errors in measuring angles with a protractor

misconceptions.statement: Any three lengths can be the sides of a triangle.
misconceptions.why: Students have drawn many triangles and never tried lengths that fail.
misconceptions.fix: A triangle exists only if the sum of any two sides is greater than the third side.

probe.question: Can a triangle have sides 2 cm, 3 cm and 8 cm?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, any three lengths make a triangle

misconceptions.root_belief: any parts can be put together freely
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student understanding of the triangle inequality

misconceptions.statement: Sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 7 cm make a triangle because 3 + 4 is not less than 7.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'not smaller' is good enough and do not picture the flat result.
misconceptions.fix: The sum of two sides must be greater than the third. If it is equal, the arcs only touch and the 'triangle' collapses into a straight line.

probe.question: Can a triangle have sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 7 cm?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because 3 + 4 = 7

misconceptions.root_belief: equal is close enough to count

misconceptions.statement: In an SAS construction, the given angle can be at any vertex, not necessarily between the two given sides.
misconceptions.why: Students remember 'two sides and an angle' and forget that the angle must be included.
misconceptions.fix: In SAS the angle lies between the two given sides. Draw one side, make the angle at one end, then mark the second side along the new arm.

probe.question: Sides AB = 5 cm and BC = 4 cm and angle A = 50 degrees are given. Is this an SAS case?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, two sides and an angle are given

misconceptions.root_belief: order and position do not matter
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student difficulties with triangle congruence conditions such as SSA

misconceptions.statement: The three angles of a triangle add up to 360 degrees.
misconceptions.why: Students mix this up with the 360 degrees of a full turn or of a quadrilateral.
misconceptions.fix: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees.

probe.question: Two angles of a triangle are 50 and 60 degrees. What is the third angle?
probe.wrong_answer: 250 degrees

misconceptions.root_belief: a fact about one shape works for all shapes

misconceptions.statement: Knowing all three angles of a triangle is enough to construct that exact triangle.
misconceptions.why: Students think three pieces of information always fix a triangle, as with three sides.
misconceptions.fix: Three angles fix only the shape, not the size, so many triangles of different sizes fit. At least one side is needed.

probe.question: A triangle has angles 40, 60 and 80 degrees. Is there only one such triangle?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, three angles fix the triangle

misconceptions.root_belief: same shape means same size
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student reasoning about conditions that determine a triangle

misconceptions.statement: The hypotenuse of a right triangle is always the horizontal bottom side.
misconceptions.why: Textbook pictures usually show the right triangle standing on its longest side or with legs on the axes.
misconceptions.fix: The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, whichever way the triangle is turned.

probe.question: A right triangle is drawn with its right angle at the top and a slanted side at the bottom. Which is the hypotenuse?
probe.wrong_answer: The bottom side

misconceptions.root_belief: the usual picture is the only valid one
misconceptions.source_hint: research on prototype effects in recognising right triangles and their parts

misconceptions.statement: In a right triangle, the right angle lies between the hypotenuse and one of the other sides.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up 'the side opposite the right angle' with 'a side next to it'.
misconceptions.fix: The right angle is between the two shorter sides (legs). The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.

probe.question: In RHS construction, where do you place the right angle, relative to the hypotenuse?
probe.wrong_answer: At one end of the hypotenuse

misconceptions.root_belief: opposite and adjacent mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Two arcs drawn from different centres can cross at only one point.
misconceptions.why: Students only look at the visible side and miss the second crossing point.
misconceptions.fix: Two arcs from different centres can cross at two points, one on each side of the line joining the centres. Either point can be used.

probe.question: Arcs of equal radius are drawn from both ends of a segment on both sides. How many crossing points are there?
probe.wrong_answer: One

misconceptions.root_belief: one situation has one single answer

misconceptions.statement: A line segment and a line are the same, so a segment goes on forever.
misconceptions.why: In everyday speech a 'line' just means a drawn stroke, and the ends of a pencil mark are not noticed.
misconceptions.fix: A line segment has two end points and a fixed length. A line has no ends and goes on both ways forever.

probe.question: Can you measure the length of a line with a ruler?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a line has a length like a segment

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's confusion between line, ray and segment
